profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a mid-sized law school's jurisprudence center between a faculty lead and the law library's innovation specialist. They are preparing candidate angles for a grant-backed workshop series and accompanying white paper based on the seed topic, focused on how AI may reshape legal positivism across legal education, legal research, and legal practice. The immediate agenda is to generate 3-4 promising framing approaches, examples, and workshop components that can appeal to both academic and practitioner audiences. The expected outcome is a short list of viable themes and a rough plan for what to include in the concept note, not a final program design.

members.name: Dr. Helena Ward
members.role: Associate Professor of Jurisprudence and Workshop Faculty Lead
members.expertise: legal theory, legal positivism, jurisprudence pedagogy, interdisciplinary academic writing
members.background: Helena teaches jurisprudence and legal method at the law school and has published on Hart, Raz, and the institutional structure of legal authority; she is leading the academic framing for an upcoming public-facing workshop series.
members.private_state: She wants the workshop to remain intellectually serious and legible to legal theorists, while still sounding contemporary enough to secure internal funding and attract practitioners.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'practice,' they usually mean adjudication, statutory interpretation, and formal legal reasoning by judges and appellate lawyers rather than back-office legal operations.
A 'useful example' in a jurisprudence workshop should be one that illuminates the rule of recognition, legal validity, or authority, even if it is not the most operationally common AI use case.
If they 'pilot' something in the white paper or workshop, that means a bounded academic demonstration or teaching module, not deployment inside live client-facing legal work.
The 'core materials' for the concept note naturally refer to canonical jurisprudence texts plus a few recent AI-law articles, because the audience needs a theory anchor before applications.

members.name: Marcus Chen
members.role: Director of Legal Innovation and Research Services
members.expertise: legal tech implementation, research workflows, practitioner training, law library innovation strategy
members.background: Marcus supports faculty and clinics with legal research platforms, AI policy pilots, and practitioner-oriented training; he regularly interfaces with firms, courts, and vendors about responsible legal AI use.
members.private_state: He wants the workshop to produce tangible, implementation-relevant outputs that demonstrate the law school's relevance to practice and justify future investment in legal innovation programming.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'practice,' they usually include legal research workflows, document review, drafting support, intake triage, compliance, and other day-to-day professional tasks beyond courtroom reasoning.
A 'useful example' should be recognizable to practitioners immediately and tied to existing AI tools or workflows they are already experimenting with.
If they 'pilot' something, that implies a small real-world institutional test, such as a clinic protocol, research guide, or practitioner training exercise that people can actually use.

The 'core materials' for a workshop concept note should include current vendor policies, court guidance on AI use, bar ethics opinions, and practical case studies, because that is what makes the event credible outside the academy.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss AI's effect on 'legal practice' as if they mean the same thing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means doctrinal and institutional legal practice centered on courts, judges, appellate argument, and questions of legal validity and authority.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader legal services ecosystem, including research platforms, drafting tools, intake, compliance, due diligence, and internal knowledge work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both domains are commonly called 'legal practice,' and in a brainstorming meeting the broad phrase sounds sufficiently shared that neither person feels a need to narrow it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that one promising idea could be 'piloted' after the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a pilot would be a classroom exercise, reading packet, or simulated jurisprudence lab used in a seminar or workshop breakout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes a pilot would be a live operational trial, such as an AI-assisted research protocol in the clinic or a practitioner-facing training module with actual users.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The verb 'pilot' is positive and flexible in academic settings, so both can endorse it without specifying whether the test environment is pedagogical or operational.

misalignment_points.topic: What should go into the core materials
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to assembling the 'core materials' for the concept note and workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of Hart's 'The Concept of Law,' Raz on authority, selected critiques of positivism, and a few theoretical AI-law articles.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of current court standing orders on AI use, bar association ethics guidance, vendor terms, law firm policies, and applied case studies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sets of documents are plausible 'core materials' for a workshop on AI and legal theory, so the phrase creates false consensus while hiding entirely different document lists.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They screen ideas by asking whether an example is 'workable' or 'strong enough' for the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 judges workability by whether the example cleanly surfaces jurisprudential questions about legal validity, authority, and the separation of law and morality.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 judges workability by whether the example is concrete, current, easy for non-theorists to grasp, and likely to produce actionable discussion for practitioners.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming, evaluating ideas as 'workable' sounds routine and cooperative; because both are indeed filtering for quality, the fact that they use different criteria remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: This has to sound timely without collapsing into a generic 'AI in law' event. If we can frame legal positivism as the intellectual spine, we can keep the workshop credible to jurisprudence colleagues and still make it attractive to the funding committee. By legal practice, I mean the sites where legal authority is actually articulated and tested—courts, judicial reasoning, appellate argument, interpretive method. I want Marcus to help make it sound outward-facing, but the center of gravity should remain doctrinal and institutional.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Marcus. I think this workshop series could be a real opportunity to connect legal positivism to AI across legal education, legal research, and legal practice in a way that feels both serious and current. At this stage, I'd love to identify a few framing angles that could hold together for a concept note and also speak to more than one audience. What feels most promising to you?

turns.inner_thought: We need this to land beyond faculty already interested in jurisprudence. If we can tie it to tools and workflows people are already using, the school can show practical relevance and maybe build a case for future innovation funding. Legal practice here should clearly include the everyday work: research platforms, drafting assistance, intake, compliance, internal review. A workable angle has to be concrete enough that a clinic director, librarian, or firm KM person immediately sees why it matters.
turns.utterance: I think the strongest directions will be the ones that resonate with faculty and practitioners at the same time. There are some fertile entry points around research tools, drafting systems, and also the court-facing concerns people are already talking about. If we can frame those in a way that feels genuinely useful rather than just topical, that gives us a lot to work with.

turns.inner_thought: Good—court-facing concerns gives me a path back to formal authority. One angle I like is whether AI reinforces a picture of law as rule-governed output, especially where legal actors are expected to justify conclusions through recognizable sources and forms of reasoning. That gets us toward validity, pedigree, and authority without sounding too abstract at the outset. That feels strong enough because it opens jurisprudential questions cleanly.
turns.utterance: One angle that strikes me as especially promising is whether AI ends up intensifying a positivist cast of mind—encouraging lawyers to treat legal outputs as more rule-bound and artifact-like than they might otherwise. That could be quite powerful if we connect it to legal practice rather than keeping it at the level of abstract theory.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that can work if we don't leave it hovering over theory. People will grasp it immediately if the discussion is tied to things like AI-assisted research memos, intake triage, citation checking, drafting support—tasks they already see in demos or daily workflow. Those are workable because they're current and recognizable, and they make the school look engaged with the real ecosystem.
turns.utterance: I like that. The same angle could land very well if we anchor it in examples people already encounter. Things connected to research memos, intake, or citation checking would help make the discussion feel immediate, and then the theoretical question doesn't seem bolted on.

turns.inner_thought: We need to be selective. Not every practical example illuminates the jurisprudential issue. The best ones are those that expose how a legal actor identifies what counts as a valid source or authoritative reason. If we can build a module around source identification and legal validity, that gives the workshop real conceptual discipline. That's the kind of example that is genuinely workable for this audience.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think we should probably discipline ourselves to two or three really workable examples rather than a long list. One strong option, at least to my mind, would be a module around how AI affects the identification of valid legal sources. That seems capable of carrying more than one strand of the discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Two or three is right, and if one of them is strong enough we should turn it into something the institution can actually use afterward. A pilot, ideally, would mean a small operational test—maybe with clinic researchers, a training session, or a research-services workflow. That would show value quickly. Her source-identification idea could possibly translate if framed through an actual task people perform.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if one of those examples proves strong enough, I could also see us piloting it after the workshop. That would help show some institutional value rather than having the whole thing end when the event ends.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot after the workshop makes sense, as long as it stays bounded and controlled. I am thinking of a compact teaching exercise or structured breakout—something with a defined prompt, a curated packet, maybe a simulated problem about identifying authority. That would let participants test the idea without pretending we're rolling anything out into live legal work. Nicely fundable, low-risk, intellectually coherent.
turns.utterance: Yes, I would be very comfortable mentioning that in the concept note. We could describe a compact follow-on format that lets participants test the idea in a controlled setting. That makes it feel developmental without overcommitting us.

turns.inner_thought: Good—that language works for a small implementation too. If we structure the session around current guidance people actually rely on, participants can leave with something usable in their organizations. I want the workshop to produce materials that map onto real policies, tool constraints, and practical scenarios. That's what will make a pilot worthwhile and the examples feel strong enough to matter outside the room.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And that becomes even more compelling if we build the session around current professional guidance and examples people can actually take back to their organizations. It helps the workshop feel grounded and gives the pilot a clearer value proposition.

turns.inner_thought: Before this drifts too far into compliance language, I need to secure the theoretical anchor. The core materials should center on Hart, Raz, perhaps a critical counterpoint or two, and then a very selective set of AI-law pieces. Otherwise the concept note will read like a generic responsible-tech event. If the foundations of positivism are clear, the applications can sit on top of them.
turns.utterance: Before we draft too much prose, I think it would help to assemble the core materials so the framing stays anchored in the foundations of positivism rather than drifting into generic tech commentary. If we get that base right, the rest should be easier to shape.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely—core materials are essential, but for me that means the documents people in the field are already using: court guidance on AI, bar ethics opinions, vendor and platform policies, practical examples. If those are in the package, the workshop will look credible to practitioners and administrators, not just academics. I can gather those quickly.
turns.utterance: I agree. Pulling together the core materials early will help us keep the package coherent. And I do think recent court guidance, ethics opinions, and platform policies should be in there, because they make the whole thing immediately credible to people outside the academy as well.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine as supplementary material, so long as the overall structure remains conceptually ordered. A three-part design gives us a clean grant narrative: education, research, practice. In the practice section, I want to show how AI unsettles the relation between finding law and interpreting authority—precisely the kind of issue legal theorists care about. That is the workable through-line.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. In terms of structure, I can imagine a three-part arc covering education, research, and practice. The practice section, in particular, could show how AI may blur the line between locating law and interpreting authority, which feels like a useful way to connect the contemporary questions back to the jurisprudential core.

turns.inner_thought: Great, we have enough to move. I'll draft something example-rich with practical materials and pilot options that could feasibly become a clinic protocol, research guide, or training exercise. Helena can provide the conceptual framing so the proposal reads as more than applied tech policy. As long as we both keep using the same umbrella language, this should come together smoothly.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a strong set of directions. Why don't I sketch some example-rich materials and a few pilot possibilities, and then you can shape the conceptual through-line across the three sections. That should give us a short list of viable themes for the concept note without forcing us to settle every detail yet.
